_note: Kinds of storylines. link_window_days = how long after the latest stage a new report still belongs to the same story, and how long follow-up search keeps looking. Each window is a judgment prior with its reason; GET /v1/calibration reports observed gaps between stages so the prior can be replaced by data (rule in docs/07-coverage-and-settings.md). 'title' is the plain-English name shown to people (website, suggestions). 'research' = published findings on how markets usually react to this kind of event (shown with their source); 'watch' = what investors typically check next, from common analyst practice. 'expectations' = the usual share price move per case (the company's part in a deal, the results reading, or how the event started), each with its source; without one, the opening stage's price expectation applies. 'flat' = no unusual move expected.
late_report_why: Outlets publish the same events in a different order than they happened (e.g. 'interim CEO in charge' before the resignation story). A resolved story therefore still absorbs reports of its earlier stages published within 3 days of its latest stage; later ones start a new story. 3 days covers same-week reporting across time zones (US and Australian outlets) without merging a new crisis weeks later.

playbooks.title: Leadership change
playbooks.description: Leader under pressure (misconduct report or public apology), then departure, then succession. Stages can follow within days (e.g. a conduct report and a resignation in the same week). A new leader named on its own (a planned succession) also starts one: a new chief executive at a large company is market-moving news (e.g. CSL named Deborah Waterhouse CEO on 21 Oct 2026, which no event caught before).
playbooks.window_why: Interim leaders are usually named at or soon after a departure, while a permanent successor search can take months. 60 days links the departure to an interim or announced successor without merging unrelated leadership news months later. Fast sequences (pressure to resignation within a week, interim CEO the same day) are common; they stay in one story and their overlapping reactions are measured together (methodology.json overlap_trading_days).

decisions.decision: pay closer attention and question their trust in management
buy insurance against a fall while the facts are unclear
flag the risk, but mostly keep their ratings until the facts are clear
order an internal review
investigate the leader's conduct
rethink the investment; some sell shares
pay more to protect against big price moves
lower ratings and price targets because the company depends on its leader
review their contracts and plans with the company
try to win its staff and customers during the change
feel less uncertain and judge the new leader
reconsider how much extra interest to demand

research.finding: Share price swings rise after a CEO change, more so when the departure is forced, and settle once the succession is clear.
research.source: Clayton, Hartzell & Rosenberg (2005), Journal of Business

research.finding: After a forced CEO change, company performance tends to improve, more so when the successor comes from outside.
research.source: Huson, Malatesta & Parrino (2004), Journal of Financial Economics

watch: Forced or planned: a forced exit carries more uncertainty than a planned retirement.
Who leads next: interim or permanent, insider or outsider.
Analyst rating and forecast changes in the following days.
The board's stated reason and any regulator or legal follow-up.

expectations.label: starts with the leader under pressure
expectations.finding: Share price swings rise after a CEO change, more so when the departure is forced.
expectations.source: Clayton, Hartzell & Rosenberg (2005), Journal of Business

expectations.label: starts with the leader stepping down
expectations.finding: Share price swings rise after a CEO change, more so when the departure is forced.
expectations.source: Clayton, Hartzell & Rosenberg (2005), Journal of Business

expectations.label: a new leader named (planned succession)
expectations.finding: Share price swings settle once the succession is clear.
expectations.source: Clayton, Hartzell & Rosenberg (2005), Journal of Business

playbooks.title: Product safety
playbooks.description: Product defect escalating from recall to regulatory action to litigation.
playbooks.window_why: Regulator probes and lawsuits tend to follow a recall by weeks to months rather than days, so a shorter window would split one safety story into several.

decisions.decision: estimate the cost of repairs and refunds
cut their profit forecasts
delay purchases or switch to rivals
win customers who switch
expect fines and orders to fix the problem
demand more interest because of possible legal costs
pay more to protect against big price moves
set money aside for possible damages
set money aside for legal costs, and may cut share buybacks

research.finding: Product recalls lead to share price losses that are often larger than the direct cost of the recall, and can spread to competitors.
research.source: Jarrell & Peltzman (1985), Journal of Political Economy

watch: Scale: number of units, injuries, countries.
Whether a regulator opens an investigation or orders more action.
Lawsuits and the company's estimate of the cost.
Competitors' share prices (the problem may affect the whole product type).

playbooks.title: Takeover
playbooks.window_why: Deal rumours that become deals are typically confirmed within about a quarter; after that we treat the rumour as faded and a new report starts a new story.

decisions.decision: buy shares of the possible target, depending on how likely the deal is
bet on a quick price rise
buy the target and sell the buyer
judge whether the buyer is paying too much

research.finding: Takeover targets' shares typically jump when a deal is announced; buyers' shares on average move little or fall.
research.source: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford (2001), Journal of Economic Perspectives

research.finding: After a deal is announced, the gap between the share price and the offer price reflects how likely the market thinks the deal is to fail.

watch: Is the company the target or the buyer? The reactions differ.
Offer price compared with the current share price.
Regulator and shareholder approvals, and any rival bid.
Whether the report is confirmed by the company (rumours often fade).

expectations.label: company is the target
expectations.finding: Takeover targets' shares typically jump when a deal is announced or reported, because buyers pay a premium.
expectations.source: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford (2001), Journal of Economic Perspectives

expectations.label: company is the buyer
expectations.finding: Buyers' shares on average move little around a deal announcement (a small fall, not reliably different from zero).
expectations.source: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford (2001), Journal of Economic Perspectives

expectations.label: company sells a unit or assets
expectations.finding: Companies selling a unit or assets gain a little on average when the sale is announced.

expectations.label: company's part unclear
expectations.finding: Targets jump and buyers move little; without knowing the company's side, only a larger-than-usual move is expected.
expectations.source: Andrade, Mitchell & Stafford (2001), Journal of Economic Perspectives

playbooks.title: Results
playbooks.description: A results or guidance release. One event per release: its reports say whether it was better or worse than expected, or both ('beat estimates, yet the outlook disappointed'), so a mixed release is one event, not two contradicting ones (seen on the live feed: Atlassian, AGL, Telstra, Nov 2026).
playbooks.window_why: Analysts revise forecasts and guidance updates land within weeks of a results release, inside one reporting cycle.

decisions.decision: re-price the shares on the news
revise their profit forecasts
pay closer attention

research.finding: Trading volume and the size of price moves rise sharply in the week of an earnings announcement.
After an earnings surprise, share prices tend to keep drifting in the direction of the surprise for weeks.
research.source: Bernard & Thomas (1989), Journal of Accounting Research

watch: Guidance for the next period: a beat with weaker guidance can still fall.
Analyst forecast revisions over the next one to two weeks.
Whether revenue, not only profit, beat expectations, and whether a miss is one-off (costs) or lasting (demand).

expectations.label: better than expected
expectations.finding: Shares move in the direction of an earnings surprise, and keep drifting that way for weeks.
expectations.source: Bernard & Thomas (1989), Journal of Accounting Research

expectations.label: worse than expected
expectations.finding: Shares move in the direction of an earnings surprise, and keep drifting that way for weeks.
expectations.source: Bernard & Thomas (1989), Journal of Accounting Research

expectations.label: mixed (e.g. profit beat, outlook disappointed)
expectations.finding: Trading volume and the size of price moves rise sharply in the week of an earnings announcement.

playbooks.absorbs_why: Results releases routinely announce the dividend and any buyback; the share price reacts to the release as a whole (Bernard & Thomas 1989 measure the announcement, not its parts), so they are one event. Seen on the live feed: Xero and Telstra, 2026-11-17.

playbooks.title: Cyber incident
playbooks.description: A data breach or major outage, which can lead to regulators and lawsuits.
playbooks.window_why: Regulator inquiries and class actions typically follow a breach disclosure by weeks to months.

decisions.decision: sell shares until the damage is known
pay more to protect against big price moves
review whether to keep using the company
expect fines
set money aside for legal costs

research.finding: Cyberattacks lower share prices on average, with larger losses when customers' personal financial information is taken.
research.source: Kamiya, Kang, Kim, Milidonis & Stulz (2021), Journal of Financial Economics

watch: What data was taken and how many customers are affected.
How long systems are down.
Regulator inquiries, fines and class actions.
Customer losses mentioned in later updates or results.

playbooks.title: Job cuts
playbooks.window_why: Details of job cuts (numbers, sites, costs) usually emerge within weeks of the first report.

decisions.decision: weigh cost savings against weaker demand; on average they sell
pay closer attention
watch for service disruptions

research.finding: Layoff announcements are met with share price falls on average, especially when the cuts come from financial trouble rather than a planned restructuring.
research.source: Worrell, Davidson & Sharma (1991), Academy of Management Journal

watch: The reason given: falling demand, cost savings, or restructuring.
Size of the cuts compared with the workforce.
Expected savings, one-off costs and any change to guidance.

playbooks.title: Supply disruption
playbooks.window_why: Supply problems tend to resolve or escalate (lost sales, guidance cuts) over one to two months.

decisions.decision: expect lower sales
switch to other suppliers
win customers who switch

research.finding: Announcements of supply chain disruptions are followed by large share price falls, and the damage often lasts.
research.source: Hendricks & Singhal (2003), Journal of Operations Management

watch: How long the disruption lasts and what share of supply it affects.
Alternative suppliers and stock on hand.
Guidance cuts or lost sales in later updates.
Suppliers and competitors exposed to the same problem.

playbooks.title: Legal & regulatory
playbooks.description: A regulator probe, fine or order, or a lawsuit against the company, then its outcome. Opens only when no product safety or cyber event of the company is open (those absorb their own regulator and lawsuit steps). Added 2026-11-17: 41 such articles about 13 of our companies (Intel shareholder suits, Meta's Italy fine, Nvidia DOJ probes, ASIC suing CBA) had opened no event.
playbooks.window_why: Probes and lawsuits take months to settle or be decided, and follow-on suits arrive in waves after the first. 180 days keeps a case, its copycat suits and its outcome in one story; a new case after that starts a new one.

decisions.decision: price in fines, damages and legal costs, and the damage to reputation
pay more to protect against big price moves
feel less uncertain once the cost is known

research.finding: When regulators act against a company for misconduct, it loses far more value than the fine itself, mostly through lost reputation.
research.source: Karpoff, Lee & Martin (2008), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

research.finding: Companies lose value on average when a lawsuit against them is filed, more so in disputes with the government.

watch: Size of the possible fine or damages compared with the company's yearly profit.
Who acts: a regulator, the government or private plaintiffs (class actions often follow a share price fall).
Whether the company disputes it, settles, or sets money aside.
Similar actions in other countries.

expectations.label: a regulator acts
expectations.finding: When regulators act against a company for misconduct, it loses far more value than the fine itself, mostly through lost reputation.
expectations.source: Karpoff, Lee & Martin (2008), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

expectations.label: a lawsuit is filed
expectations.finding: Companies lose value on average when a lawsuit against them is filed, more so in disputes with the government.

expectations.label: a regulator and lawsuits
expectations.finding: When regulators act against a company for misconduct, it loses far more value than the fine itself, mostly through lost reputation.
expectations.source: Karpoff, Lee & Martin (2008), Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

playbooks.title: Dividends & buybacks
playbooks.description: A change in what the company pays back to shareholders: a dividend raised, cut, started or stopped, a special dividend, or a share buyback announced or halted. Added 2026-11-17: 11 such articles about 7 of our companies (Costco's special dividend and buyback, ExxonMobil's raise and buyback) had opened no event.
playbooks.window_why: Details (amount, dates, how it is funded) follow the announcement within weeks; the next payout decision comes with the next results and starts a new event.

decisions.decision: read it as management's view of future cash flows
buy for a higher payout, or sell after a cut

research.finding: Shares rise when a company starts or raises its dividend and fall sharply when it cuts or stops it: payouts are read as a signal about future earnings.
research.source: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Journal of Finance

research.finding: Shares rise when a buyback is announced, and tend to keep doing better than the market for years after.
research.source: Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1995), Journal of Financial Economics

watch: Size of the change compared with last year's payout.
Whether it is paid from cash flow or from debt.
What management says about future earnings.
For Australian shares: franking credits.

expectations.label: raised, special or buyback
expectations.finding: Shares rise when a company starts or raises its dividend and fall sharply when it cuts or stops it: payouts are read as a signal about future earnings. Buybacks too: shares rise when a buyback is announced, and tend to keep doing better than the market for years after.
expectations.source: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Journal of Finance; Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1995), Journal of Financial Economics

expectations.label: cut or stopped
expectations.finding: Shares rise when a company starts or raises its dividend and fall sharply when it cuts or stops it: payouts are read as a signal about future earnings.
expectations.source: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Journal of Finance

expectations.label: mixed (e.g. dividend cut, buyback added)
expectations.finding: Shares rise when a company starts or raises its dividend and fall sharply when it cuts or stops it: payouts are read as a signal about future earnings.
expectations.source: Michaely, Thaler & Womack (1995), Journal of Finance
